claim: Amyloid-β peptide (Aβ) forms plaques in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Amyloid-β peptide (Aβ) forms plaques in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is responsible for early cognitive deficits in AD patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology cited in the abstract.

claim: Aβ is responsible for early cognitive deficits in AD patients.
source: Amyloid-β peptide (Aβ) forms plaques in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is responsible for early cognitive deficits in AD patients.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific literature on AD.

claim: Advancing cognitive decline is accompanied by progressive impairment of cognition-relevant EEG patterns such as gamma oscillations.
source: Advancing cognitive decline is accompanied by progressive impairment of cognition-relevant EEG patterns such as gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about AD progression and EEG patterns.

claim: The endocannabinoid anandamide is a TrpV1-receptor agonist.
source: The endocannabinoid anandamide, a TrpV1-receptor agonist, reverses hippocampal damage and memory impairment in rodents and protects neurons from Aβ-induced cytotoxic effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about anandamide's receptor binding properties.

claim: Anandamide reverses hippocampal damage and memory impairment in rodents.
source: The endocannabinoid anandamide, a TrpV1-receptor agonist, reverses hippocampal damage and memory impairment in rodents and protects neurons from Aβ-induced cytotoxic effects.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the abstract.

claim: Anandamide protects neurons from Aβ-induced cytotoxic effects.
source: The endocannabinoid anandamide, a TrpV1-receptor agonist, reverses hippocampal damage and memory impairment in rodents and protects neurons from Aβ-induced cytotoxic effects.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the abstract.

claim: The TrpV1-receptor agonist capsaicin rescues Aβ-induced degradation of hippocampal gamma oscillations.
source: We found that the TrpV1-receptor agonist capsaicin rescues Aβ-induced degradation of hippocampal gamma oscillations by reversing both the desynchronization of AP firing in CA3 pyramidal cells and the shift in excitatory/inhibitory current balance.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Capsaicin reverses the desynchronization of AP firing in CA3 pyramidal cells induced by Aβ.
source: We found that the TrpV1-receptor agonist capsaicin rescues Aβ-induced degradation of hippocampal gamma oscillations by reversing both the desynchronization of AP firing in CA3 pyramidal cells and the shift in excitatory/inhibitory current balance.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Capsaicin reverses the shift in excitatory/inhibitory current balance induced by Aβ.
source: We found that the TrpV1-receptor agonist capsaicin rescues Aβ-induced degradation of hippocampal gamma oscillations by reversing both the desynchronization of AP firing in CA3 pyramidal cells and the shift in excitatory/inhibitory current balance.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rescue effect of capsaicin is TrpV1-receptor-dependent.
source: This rescue effect is TrpV1-receptor-dependent since it was absent in TrpV1 knockout mice or in the presence of the TrpV1-receptor antagonist capsazepine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using TrpV1 knockout mice and the antagonist capsazepine.

claim: The rescue effect of capsaicin was absent in TrpV1 knockout mice.
source: This rescue effect is TrpV1-receptor-dependent since it was absent in TrpV1 knockout mice or in the presence of the TrpV1-receptor antagonist capsazepine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using TrpV1 knockout mice.

claim: The rescue effect of capsaicin was absent in the presence of the TrpV1-receptor antagonist capsazepine.
source: This rescue effect is TrpV1-receptor-dependent since it was absent in TrpV1 knockout mice or in the presence of the TrpV1-receptor antagonist capsazepine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using the antagonist capsazepine.

claim: AD is an irreversible progressive neurodegenerative disorder.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the most common type of dementia in the elderly (Brookmeyer et al., 2007; Qiu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD supported by citations.

claim: AD is the most common type of dementia in the elderly.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the most common type of dementia in the elderly (Brookmeyer et al., 2007; Qiu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD supported by citations.

claim: AD is characterized by a progressive deficit in cognition, principally in memory and learning.
source: AD is characterized by a progressive deficit in cognition, principally in memory and learning and has become a major public health challenge.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD symptoms.

claim: Aβ is the main component of senile plaques in AD.
source: Today, there are several lines of evidence indicating that amyloid-β peptide (Aβ), the main component of senile plaques in AD, plays an important role in AD pathogenesis and is responsible for the early cognitive deficit observed in the disease with the Aβ1–42 peptide thought to be particularly disease relevant (Lue et al., 1999; Näslund et al., 2000; Walsh and Selkoe, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology supported by citations.

claim: Aβ plays an important role in AD pathogenesis.
source: Today, there are several lines of evidence indicating that amyloid-β peptide (Aβ), the main component of senile plaques in AD, plays an important role in AD pathogenesis and is responsible for the early cognitive deficit observed in the disease with the Aβ1–42 peptide thought to be particularly disease relevant (Lue et al., 1999; Näslund et al., 2000; Walsh and Selkoe, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The Aβ1–42 peptide is thought to be particularly disease relevant.
source: Today, there are several lines of evidence indicating that amyloid-β peptide (Aβ), the main component of senile plaques in AD, plays an important role in AD pathogenesis and is responsible for the early cognitive deficit observed in the disease with the Aβ1–42 peptide thought to be particularly disease relevant (Lue et al., 1999; Näslund et al., 2000; Walsh and Selkoe, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aβ induces impairments in neuronal network functions that are important for cognition, such as network oscillations.
source: Aβ has also been shown to induce impairments in neuronal network functions that are important for cognition, such as network oscillations (Driver et al., 2007; Nerelius et al., 2009; Balleza-Tapia et al., 2010; Villette et al., 2010; Gutiérrez-Lerma et al., 2013; Kurudenkandy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal network oscillations in various frequency bands are crucial for information processing in the brain.
source: Neuronal network oscillations in various frequency bands are crucial for information processing in the brain (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Gamma-frequency oscillations (30–80 Hz) have been suggested to underlie cognitive processes such as attention, sensory perception and memory.
source: In particular, gamma-frequency oscillations (30–80 Hz) have been suggested to underlie cognitive processes such as attention, sensory perception and memory (Tallon-Baudry and Bertrand, 1999; Sederberg et al., 2007; Fries, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gamma oscillations progressively decrease in AD patients in lock-step with advancing cognitive impairment.
source: This is supported by the finding that gamma oscillations progressively decrease in AD patients in lock-step with advancing cognitive impairment (Herrmann and Demiralp, 2005; Koenig et al., 2005; de Haan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Endocannabinoids such as anandamide have been shown to possess protective properties against Aβ-induced neuronal damage.
source: Endocannabinoids such as anandamide have been shown to possess protective properties against Aβ-induced neuronal damage (Aso and Ferrer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A negative correlation was found between anandamide and Aβ levels in AD brains.
source: Indeed, a negative correlation was found between anandamide and Aβ levels in AD brains (Jung et al., 2012) suggesting that the endocannabinoid's protective role is decreased in AD.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The endocannabinoid's protective role is decreased in AD.
source: Indeed, a negative correlation was found between anandamide and Aβ levels in AD brains (Jung et al., 2012) suggesting that the endocannabinoid's protective role is decreased in AD.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative correlation between anandamide and Aβ levels.

claim: Enhancement of anandamide levels by inhibition of endocannabinoid cellular reuptake can reverse hippocampal damage and memory impairment in rodents pretreated with Aβ.
source: In this context, it has been reported that enhancement of anandamide levels by inhibition of endocannabinoid cellular reuptake can reverse hippocampal damage and memory impairment in rodents pretreated with Aβ (van der Stelt et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In vitro studies have shown that anandamide can protect neurons from Aβ's neurotoxic effects.
source: Also, in vitro studies have shown that anandamide can protect neurons from Aβ's neurotoxic effects (Milton, 2002) through a mechanism independent of CB1 and CB2 activation (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Anandamide protects neurons from Aβ's neurotoxic effects through a mechanism independent of CB1 and CB2 activation.
source: Also, in vitro studies have shown that anandamide can protect neurons from Aβ's neurotoxic effects (Milton, 2002) through a mechanism independent of CB1 and CB2 activation (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Anandamide also activates the transient receptor potential cation channel/vanilloid receptor TrpV1.
source: Since anandamide also activates the transient receptor potential cation channel/vanilloid receptor TrpV1 (Aso and Ferrer, 2014), it is possible that its protective properties are mediated by this receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: It is possible that anandamide's protective properties are mediated by TrpV1 receptor.
source: Since anandamide also activates the transient receptor potential cation channel/vanilloid receptor TrpV1 (Aso and Ferrer, 2014), it is possible that its protective properties are mediated by this receptor.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the fact that anandamide activates TrpV1.

claim: TrpV1 is a ligand-gated non-selective cation channel and belongs to the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family.
source: TrpV1 is a ligand-gated non-selective cation channel and belongs to the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family (Nieto-Posadas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TrpV1 supported by a citation.

claim: TrpV1 is known to be activated by capsaicin.
source: It is known to be activated by capsaicin (Cp; Caterina et al., 1997), the pungent ingredient in hot chili peppers, but also by numerous stimuli including several endogenous lipid molecules (endovanilloids) such as anandamide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TrpV1 supported by a citation.

claim: Capsaicin is the pungent ingredient in hot chili peppers.
source: It is known to be activated by capsaicin (Cp; Caterina et al., 1997), the pungent ingredient in hot chili peppers, but also by numerous stimuli including several endogenous lipid molecules (endovanilloids) such as anandamide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about capsaicin.

claim: TrpV1 is activated by numerous stimuli including several endogenous lipid molecules (endovanilloids) such as anandamide.
source: It is known to be activated by capsaicin (Cp; Caterina et al., 1997), the pungent ingredient in hot chili peppers, but also by numerous stimuli including several endogenous lipid molecules (endovanilloids) such as anandamide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TrpV1 activation.

claim: TrpV1 has been reported to be expressed in the brain.
source: TrpV1 has been reported to be expressed in the brain (Sasamura et al., 1998; Mezey et al., 2000; Roberts et al., 2004; Tóth et al., 2005; Cristino et al., 2006) where it is involved in several functions such as the modulation of spine morphology, synaptic transmission and plasticity (Ho et al., 2012; Edwards, 2014; Martins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: TrpV1 is involved in several functions such as the modulation of spine morphology, synaptic transmission and plasticity.
source: TrpV1 has been reported to be expressed in the brain (Sasamura et al., 1998; Mezey et al., 2000; Roberts et al., 2004; Tóth et al., 2005; Cristino et al., 2006) where it is involved in several functions such as the modulation of spine morphology, synaptic transmission and plasticity (Ho et al., 2012; Edwards, 2014; Martins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aβ-induced degradation of gamma oscillations in the hippocampal network is caused by the desynchronization of action potential (AP) firing of pyramidal cells.
source: Previously, we have established that Aβ-induced degradation of gamma oscillations in the hippocampal network is caused by the desynchronization of action potential (AP) firing of pyramidal cells (PC) and a shift in the excitatory/inhibitory current balance (Kurudenkandy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Aβ-induced degradation of gamma oscillations in the hippocampal network is caused by a shift in the excitatory/inhibitory current balance.
source: Previously, we have established that Aβ-induced degradation of gamma oscillations in the hippocampal network is caused by the desynchronization of action potential (AP) firing of pyramidal cells (PC) and a shift in the excitatory/inhibitory current balance (Kurudenkandy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Hippocampal slices incubated with 50 nM Aβ and 200 nM WIN resulted in significantly reduced gamma oscillation power (64.2 ± 9.0% reduction).
source: We found that compared to hippocampal slices in control conditions (100 nM KA, power: 11.6 ± 1.7×10−9 V2, n = 32, Figure 1A–B), Aβ+WIN incubation resulted in significantly reduced gamma oscillation power (64.2 ± 9.0% reduction, power: 4.1 ± 1.0×10−9 V2, n = 18, p = 0.0002 vs. control, Figure 1A–B), that was not significantly different from the reduced gamma power recorded in slices incubated with Aβ only (59.4 ± 8.9% reduction, power: 4.7 ± 1.0×10−9 V2, n = 20, p = 0.0007 vs control, Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Aβ+WIN incubation resulted in gamma oscillation power that was not significantly different from the reduced gamma power recorded in slices incubated with Aβ only.
source: We found that compared to hippocampal slices in control conditions (100 nM KA, power: 11.6 ± 1.7×10−9 V2, n = 32, Figure 1A–B), Aβ+WIN incubation resulted in significantly reduced gamma oscillation power (64.2 ± 9.0% reduction, power: 4.1 ± 1.0×10−9 V2, n = 18, p = 0.0002 vs. control, Figure 1A–B), that was not significantly different from the reduced gamma power recorded in slices incubated with Aβ only (59.4 ± 8.9% reduction, power: 4.7 ± 1.0×10−9 V2, n = 20, p = 0.0007 vs control, Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Slices incubated with Aβ only showed 59.4 ± 8.9% reduction in gamma power.
source: We found that compared to hippocampal slices in control conditions (100 nM KA, power: 11.6 ± 1.7×10−9 V2, n = 32, Figure 1A–B), Aβ+WIN incubation resulted in significantly reduced gamma oscillation power (64.2 ± 9.0% reduction, power: 4.1 ± 1.0×10−9 V2, n = 18, p = 0.0002 vs. control, Figure 1A–B), that was not significantly different from the reduced gamma power recorded in slices incubated with Aβ only (59.4 ± 8.9% reduction, power: 4.7 ± 1.0×10−9 V2, n = 20, p = 0.0007 vs control, Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-B.

claim: When incubating hippocampal slices with 50 nM Aβ and CB1 agonist ACEA (200 nM, 15 min), gamma oscillations showed a significant reduction in power (49.9 ± 6.9% reduction).
source: Likewise, when incubating hippocampal slices with 50 nM Aβ and a specific agonist for CB1 (ACEA, 200 nM, 15 min), we found that gamma oscillations continued to show a significant reduction in power (49.9 ± 6.9% reduction, power: 5.8 ± 0.8×10−9 V2, n = 21, p = 0.0062 vs. control, Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-B.

claim: When a specific CB2 agonist (JWH; 100 nM) was used with Aβ, a 48.0 ± 13.5% reduction in gamma power was observed.
source: Similar results were obtained when a specific CB2 agonist (JWH; 100 nM) was used (48.0 ± 13.5% reduction, power: 6.0 ± 1.6×10−9 V2, n = 10, p = 0.0265 vs control, Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Even when increasing WIN concentration to 1 µM no protective effect against Aβ-induced gamma oscillation reduction was observed.
source: Even when increasing WIN concentration to 1 µM no protective effect against Aβ-induced gamma oscillation reduction was observed (58.9 ± 15.4% reduction, power: 4.8 ± 1.8×10−9 V2, n = 5, p = 0.0326 vs control).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cannabinoid receptor activation does not exert a protective effect against Aβ-induced impairment of functional network dynamics in hippocampus.
source: All together, these data indicate that cannabinoid receptor activation does not exert a protective effect against Aβ-induced impairment of functional network dynamics in hippocampus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing no protective effect of CB1/CB2 agonists.

claim: Incubation with 50 nM Aβ and 10 µM capsaicin (Cp, 15 min) completely prevented the Aβ-induced reduction of gamma power.
source: In contrast to cannabinoid receptor activation, we found that incubation with 50 nM Aβ and 10 µM of the TrpV1 receptor agonist capsaicin (Cp, 15 min) completely prevented the Aβ-induced reduction of gamma power (control: 11.6 ± 1.7×10−9 V2, n = 32; Aβ+Cp: 11.8 ± 1.8×10−9 V2, n = 18; p = 0.2961; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Gamma oscillation power was significantly reduced in hippocampal slices incubated with capsazepine (Cz) together with Aβ and Cp compared to control.
source: Gamma oscillation power was significantly reduced in hippocampal slices incubated with Cz together with Aβ and Cp compared to control (Aβ+Cz, power: 4.2 ± 0.92×10−9 V2, n = 7, p = 0.0122 vs control, Figure 1C–D) indicating that TrpV1 receptor activation mediates the protective properties of Cp.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C-D.

claim: TrpV1 receptor activation mediates the protective properties of Cp.
source: Gamma oscillation power was significantly reduced in hippocampal slices incubated with Cz together with Aβ and Cp compared to control (Aβ+Cz, power: 4.2 ± 0.92×10−9 V2, n = 7, p = 0.0122 vs control, Figure 1C–D) indicating that TrpV1 receptor activation mediates the protective properties of Cp.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the TrpV1 antagonist blocks Cp's protective effect.

claim: Gamma oscillation power was significantly reduced when hippocampal slices were incubated with Aβ and only Cz.
source: Similarly, gamma oscillation power was significantly reduced when hippocampal slices were incubated with Aβ and only Cz (Aβ+Cz, power: 2.2 ± 0.38×10−9 V2, n = 14, p < 0.0001 vs control, Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C-D.

claim: 50 nM Aβ significantly reduced the coefficient of rhythmicity (Cr) compared to control.
source: Concomitantly with decreasing gamma power, 50 nM Aβ significantly reduced Cr compared to control (control Cr: 0.50 ± 0.01, Aβ Cr: 0.45 ± 0.02, p = 0.0149, Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The loss of rhythmicity caused by Aβ suggests an alteration in the synchronization of hippocampal cellular activity.
source: This loss of rhythmicity caused by Aβ suggests an alteration in the synchronization of hippocampal cellular activity, which correlates with our previous findings (Kurudenkandy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Cr and supported by prior research.

claim: Cp treatment prevented the Aβ-induced reduction of Cr.
source: Subsequent Cp treatment prevented the Aβ-induced reduction of Cr (Aβ+Cp Cr: 0.50 ± 0.02, p = 0.4003 vs control, Figure 1F–G) in a TrpV1-dependent manner since addition of Cz blocked the Cp protective effect (Aβ+Cp+Cz Cr: 0.42 ± 0.02, p = 0.0061 vs control, Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Addition of Cz blocked the Cp protective effect on Cr.
source: Subsequent Cp treatment prevented the Aβ-induced reduction of Cr (Aβ+Cp Cr: 0.50 ± 0.02, p = 0.4003 vs control, Figure 1F–G) in a TrpV1-dependent manner since addition of Cz blocked the Cp protective effect (Aβ+Cp+Cz Cr: 0.42 ± 0.02, p = 0.0061 vs control, Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F-G.

claim: TrpV1 receptor activation prevents Aβ-induced reduction of gamma oscillations through a mechanism affecting the synchrony of hippocampal cellular activity.
source: These data suggest that TrpV1 receptor activation prevents Aβ-induced reduction of gamma oscillations through a mechanism affecting the synchrony of hippocampal cellular activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Cr and synchronization.

claim: Aβ together with Cz did not affect gamma rhythmicity since no reduction in Cr was found.
source: Interestingly, Aβ together with Cz did not affect gamma rhythmicity since no reduction in Cr was found (Aβ+Cz Cr: 0.50 ± 0.03, p = 0.4572 vs control, Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Cp treatment alone induced a 66.5 ± 7.3% reduction of gamma power compared to control.
source: Interestingly, we found than Cp treatment alone induced a 66.5 ± 7.3% reduction of gamma power compared to control (control: 17.5 ± 3.1×10−9 V2, n = 14; Cp: 5.9 ± 1.3×10−9 V2, n = 7; p = 0.005; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When hippocampal slices were incubated with 10 µM Cp and 10 µM Cz (15 min), the resulting gamma oscillations remained depressed and were not significantly different from the results obtained with Cp alone.
source: To determine if this inhibitory effect of Cp was mediated via activation of TrpV1 receptors, we incubated hippocampal slices with 10 µM Cp and 10 µM Cz (15 min). The resulting gamma oscillations remained depressed and were not significantly different from the results obtained with Cp alone (63.2 ± 7.0% reduction, Cp+Cz, power: 6.4 ± 1.2×10−9 V2, n = 15, p = 0.0014 vs control, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cp activates two different, independent pathways: a TrpV1-dependent one, which mediates the protective effect of Cp against Aβ-induced reduction of gamma oscillations, and a TrpV1-independent one, which mediates the reduction of gamma oscillations caused by Cp itself.
source: Our data show that Cp activates two different, independent pathways: a TrpV1-dependent one, which mediates the protective effect of Cp against Aβ-induced reduction of gamma oscillations, and a TrpV1-independent one, which mediates the reduction of gamma oscillations caused by Cp itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing different effects of Cp with and without Cz.

claim: The effect of Cp via the TrpV1-dependend pathway occludes its TrpV1-independent action in the presence of Aβ.
source: It is also apparent that the effect of Cp via the TrpV1-dependend pathway occludes its TrpV1-independent action in the presence of Aβ.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Cp protects against Aβ despite having an inhibitory effect alone.

claim: TrpV1 KO slices treated with 50 nM Aβ (15 min) displayed a 51.2 ± 11.1% reduction in gamma power compared to control slices.
source: As shown in Figure 2A–D, slices treated with 50 nM Aβ (15 min) displayed a 51.2 ± 11.1% reduction in gamma power compared to control slices (control: 3.5 ± 0.7×10−9 V2, n = 10; Aβ: 1.7 ± 0.4×10−9 V2, n = 9; p = 0.0394).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The reduction in gamma power in TrpV1 KO slices was similar to the one observed in WT slices (59.4 ± 8.9%).
source: This reduction was similar to the one observed in WT slices (59.4 ± 8.9%, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from TrpV1 KO and WT slices.

claim: In TrpV1 KO slices, 10 µM Cp treatment did not prevent the Aβ-induced reduction of gamma power.
source: As expected 10 µM Cp treatment did not prevent the Aβ-induced reduction of gamma power (Aβ+Cp: 0.9 ± 0.4×10−9 V2, n = 8; p = 0.0022 vs control, Figure 2A–D) supporting the above results on mediation of the Cp preventive effect via a TrpV1-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A-D.

claim: TrpV1 KO slices incubated with Cp and Aβ displayed a greater reduction in gamma oscillations power (73.8 ± 11.8%) compared to Aβ-only incubation.
source: Interestingly, TrpV1 KO slices incubated with Cp and Aβ displayed a greater reduction in gamma oscillations power (73.8 ± 11.8%) compared to Aβ-only incubation (Aβ: 1.7 ± 0.4×10−9 V2, n = 9; Aβ+Cp: 0.9 ± 0.4×10−9 V2, n = 8; p = 0.0296; Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The further reduction in gamma power in TrpV1 KO slices is likely due to the TrpV1-independent effect of Cp, which in the absence of the receptor is no longer occluded.
source: It is likely that this further reduction in gamma power is due to the TrpV1-independent effect of Cp observed in WT slices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which in the absence of the receptor in TrpV1 KO slices is no longer occluded.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing WT and TrpV1 KO slices.

claim: In TrpV1 KO hippocampal slices, Aβ did not reduce the quality of gamma oscillations since no changes of Cr were observed in Aβ-treated slices.
source: In contrast to the Aβ effect on Cr observed in WT slices (Figure 1G), we found that Aβ did not reduce the quality of gamma oscillations in TrpV1 KO hippocampal slices (Figure 2B) since no changes of Cr were observed in Aβ-treated slices (control Cr: 0.49 ± 0.05, Aβ Cr: 0.51 ± 0.04, p = 0.4211, Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B,D.

claim: Similar results were found in TrpV1 KO slices treated with Aβ and Cp (no change in Cr).
source: Similar results were found in slices treated with Aβ and Cp (Aβ+Cp Cr: 0.42 ± 0.06, p = 0.1185 vs control, Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: There are subtle differences in gamma oscillation characteristics in TrpV1 KO vs WT mice.
source: This suggests that there are subtle differences in gamma oscillation characteristics in TrpV1 KO vs WT mice, which are outside the focus of this study.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in Cr responses between WT and TrpV1 KO slices.

claim: 1 µM Aβ application for 15–20 min induced a 40.2 ± 7.02% reduction in gamma oscillation power.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, 1 µM Aβ application for 15–20 min induced a 40.2 ± 7.02% reduction in gamma oscillation power (control: 8.6 ± 1.5×10−10 V2, Aβ: 5.2 ± 1.1×10−10 V2, n = 11, p = 0.0005, Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A,D.

claim: In parallel with gamma power impairment, Aβ also induced a 47.2 ± 10.1% reduction in AP firing frequency of PC.
source: In parallel with gamma power impairment Aβ also induced a 47.2 ± 10.1% reduction in AP firing frequency of PC (control: 2.0 ± 0.5 Hz, Aβ: 0.9 ± 0.2 Hz, n = 10, p = 0.0068, Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A,D.

claim: No change in the membrane potential was observed after Aβ application compared to control.
source: No change in the membrane potential was observed after Aβ application compared to control (control: −40.4 ± 0.9 mV, Aβ: −40.1 ± 1.6 mV, n = 7, p = 0.3438, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Aβ application slightly changed the AP preferred phase-angle.
source: The results show that Aβ application slightly changed the AP preferred phase-angle (n = 9, control: 5.07 ± 0.02 radians, Aβ: 5.40 ± 0.04 radians, p < 0.0001, Figure 3C,D), which can be observed as a small shift to the right in the AP-phase distribution (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C,D.

claim: It is open to question whether such a small phase angle change has any functional significance.
source: It is, however, open to question whether such a small phase angle change has any functional significance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of the observed phase angle change.

claim: Aβ induced a desynchronization of PC activity that can be observed as an increase in the AP-phase Gaussian half-width of the AP firing window.
source: More importantly, Aβ induced a desynchronization of PC activity that can be observed as an increase in the AP-phase Gaussian half-width of the AP firing window (control: 3.40 ± 0.62 radians, Aβ: 4.43 ± 0.79 radians, n = 9, p = 0.0098, Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The data corroborates previous findings that Aβ-induced reduction of gamma oscillations is caused by a desynchronization of AP firing in CA3 PC.
source: Our data corroborates our previous findings, which demonstrated that Aβ-induced reduction of gamma oscillations is caused by a desynchronization of AP firing in CA3 PC (Kurudenkandy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the current experimental data and prior research.

claim: The reduction in AP firing frequency found in whole-cell recordings is in contrast with a previous study in which Aβ induced an increase of AP firing in PC recorded in the cell-attached configuration.
source: Interestingly, the reduction in AP firing frequency found here is in contrast with our previous study in which Aβ induced an increase of AP firing in PC recorded in the cell-attached configuration (Kurudenkandy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of current experimental data with prior research.

claim: When AP were recorded as unitary events extracellularly, Aβ application increased AP firing frequency as previously reported.
source: In order to investigate whether this difference in Aβ effect could be explained by the different recording configuration employed here (whole-cell patch), we recorded AP as unitary events extracellularly and found that under these conditions Aβ application increased AP firing frequency as previously reported (control: 3.8 ± 0.9 Hz, Aβ: 4.9 ± 1.6 Hz, n = 5, p = 0.0313, for experimental data see Source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: When slices were perfused with 1µM Aβ together with 10 µM Cp, there was a 34.7 ± 9.4% decrease in gamma oscillation power after 15 min.
source: We perfused slices with 1µM Aβ together with 10 µM Cp and, surprisingly, found a 34.7 ± 9.4% decrease in gamma oscillation power (control: 2.3 ± 1.1×10−10 V2, Aβ+Cp 15 min: 1.1 ± 0.3×10−10 V2, n = 6, p = 0.0313, Figure 4—figure supplement 1); similar to the reduction caused by 1 µM Aβ application alone (40.2 ± 7.02% of inhibition, Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the treatment was extended from 15 to 30 min, the reduction in gamma oscillation power persisted and even increased.
source: To test for a possible delayed action of Cp, we extended the treatment from 15 to 30 min. However, the reduction in gamma oscillation power persisted and even increased (Aβ+Cp 30 min: 42.6 ± 17.1% inhibition, power: 0.8 ± 0.3×10−10 V2, p = 0.0313 vs control, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 5 µM Cp prevented the Aβ-induced impairment of gamma oscillation power.
source: Our results show that this lower Cp concentration prevented the Aβ-induced impairment of gamma oscillation power (control: 2.8 ± 1.0×10−10 V2, Aβ+Cp: 2.6 ± 1.0×10−10 V2, n = 8, p = 0.3203, Figure 4A,D) as well as the reduction of AP firing rate (control: 0.86 ± 0.24 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 0.58 ± 0.14 Hz, n = 6, p = 0.2188, Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A,D.

claim: 5 µM Cp prevented the reduction of AP firing rate induced by Aβ.
source: Our results show that this lower Cp concentration prevented the Aβ-induced impairment of gamma oscillation power (control: 2.8 ± 1.0×10−10 V2, Aβ+Cp: 2.6 ± 1.0×10−10 V2, n = 8, p = 0.3203, Figure 4A,D) as well as the reduction of AP firing rate (control: 0.86 ± 0.24 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 0.58 ± 0.14 Hz, n = 6, p = 0.2188, Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A,D.

claim: In TrpV1 KO slices, 5 µM Cp treatment did not prevent Aβ-induced effects on gamma power.
source: In contrast, 5 µM Cp treatment did not prevent Aβ-induced effects in slices from the TrpV1 KO mice: neither on gamma power (control: 1.2 ± 0.4×10−10 V2, Aβ+Cp: 0.6 ± 0.4×10−10 V2, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 4E,H) nor on AP firing (control: 1.30 ± 0.47 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 0.17 ± 0.06 Hz, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E,H.

claim: In TrpV1 KO slices, 5 µM Cp treatment did not prevent Aβ-induced effects on AP firing.
source: In contrast, 5 µM Cp treatment did not prevent Aβ-induced effects in slices from the TrpV1 KO mice: neither on gamma power (control: 1.2 ± 0.4×10−10 V2, Aβ+Cp: 0.6 ± 0.4×10−10 V2, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 4E,H) nor on AP firing (control: 1.30 ± 0.47 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 0.17 ± 0.06 Hz, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E,H.

claim: Cp preventive effect at 5 µM is reliant on TrpV1 receptor activation.
source: This indicates that Cp preventive effect at 5 µM is reliant onTrpV1 receptor activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing WT and TrpV1 KO slices.

claim: After combined Aβ and Cp treatment, no change in membrane potential was observed in KA-activated slices of either WT or TrpV1 KO mice.
source: After combined Aβ and Cp treatment, no change in membrane potential was observed in KA-activated slices of either WT (control: −43.5 ± 1.0 mV, Aβ+Cp: −42.2 ± 2.1 mV, n = 6, p = 0.1563) or TrpV1 KO mice (control: −41.7 ± 1.4 mV, Aβ+Cp: −43.7 ± 2.0 mV, n = 6, p = 0.2188).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: 5 µM Cp treatment completely prevented the Aβ-induced desynchronization of PC activity in WT slices.
source: By analyzing AP spike-phase coupling we found that 5 µM Cp treatment completely prevented the Aβ-induced desynchronization of PC activity in WT slices (Figure 4B–D; n = 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B-D.

claim: No changes were observed in the preferred phase-angle after 5 µM Cp treatment in WT slices.
source: No changes were observed any longer in the preferred phase-angle (control: 5.46 ± 0.04 radians, Aβ+Cp: 5.42 ± 0.04 radians, p = 0.2222, Figure 4D) and the half-width of the PC fire window (control: 3.98 ± 0.71 radians, Aβ+Cp: 3.93 ± 0.91 radians, p = 0.4206, Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C,D.

claim: No changes were observed in the half-width of the PC fire window after 5 µM Cp treatment in WT slices.
source: No changes were observed any longer in the preferred phase-angle (control: 5.46 ± 0.04 radians, Aβ+Cp: 5.42 ± 0.04 radians, p = 0.2222, Figure 4D) and the half-width of the PC fire window (control: 3.98 ± 0.71 radians, Aβ+Cp: 3.93 ± 0.91 radians, p = 0.4206, Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Despite the reduction in gamma oscillation power and AP firing observed in TrpV1 KO slices, the spike-phase coupling of AP did not display any change after combined Aβ and Cp application.
source: Interestingly, despite the reduction in gamma oscillation power and AP firing observed in TrpV1 KO slices, the spike-phase coupling of AP did not display any change after combined Aβ and Cp application (Figure 4F–H, n = 6); neither in the preferred phase-angle (control: 5.49 ± 0.03 radians, Aβ+Cp: 5.37 ± 0.08 radians, p = 0.0958, Figure 4G,H) nor in the half-width of the PC fire window (control: 4.25 ± 0.53 radians, Aβ+Cp: 5.01 ± 1.03 radians, n = 0.2813, Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4F-H.

claim: The mechanism underlying the reduction of gamma oscillation power observed in TrpV1 KO slices is related to the decrease in PC activity.
source: This result suggests that the mechanism underlying the reduction of gamma oscillation power observed in TrpV1 KO slices is related to the decrease in PC activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in spike-phase coupling despite reduced gamma power.

claim: A low Cp concentration (5 µM) reverses Aβ-induced desynchronization of PC activity via a TrpV1-dependent mechanism.
source: In summary, our data suggest that a low Cp concentration (5 µM) reverses Aβ-induced desynchronization of PC activity via a TrpV1-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing WT and TrpV1 KO slices.

claim: 1 µM Aβ application induced a 22.9 +/- 9.5% reduction in EPSC amplitude.
source: As shown in Figure 5, 1 µM Aβ application induced a 22.9 +/- 9.5% reduction in EPSC amplitude (control: 26.7 ± 1.8 pA, Aβ: 21.0 ± 3.3 pA, n = 7, p = 0.0391, Figure 5A) while no effect was observed on EPCS frequency (control: 34.7 ± 2.3 Hz, Aβ: 36.7 ± 3.3 Hz, n = 7, p = 0.2891, Figure 5A) and charge transfer (control: 490.8 ± 50.8 pC, Aβ: 433.7 ± 82.6 pC, n = 7, p = 0.1875, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: No effect of Aβ was observed on EPSC frequency.
source: As shown in Figure 5, 1 µM Aβ application induced a 22.9 +/- 9.5% reduction in EPSC amplitude (control: 26.7 ± 1.8 pA, Aβ: 21.0 ± 3.3 pA, n = 7, p = 0.0391, Figure 5A) while no effect was observed on EPCS frequency (control: 34.7 ± 2.3 Hz, Aβ: 36.7 ± 3.3 Hz, n = 7, p = 0.2891, Figure 5A) and charge transfer (control: 490.8 ± 50.8 pC, Aβ: 433.7 ± 82.6 pC, n = 7, p = 0.1875, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: No effect of Aβ was observed on EPSC charge transfer.
source: As shown in Figure 5, 1 µM Aβ application induced a 22.9 +/- 9.5% reduction in EPSC amplitude (control: 26.7 ± 1.8 pA, Aβ: 21.0 ± 3.3 pA, n = 7, p = 0.0391, Figure 5A) while no effect was observed on EPCS frequency (control: 34.7 ± 2.3 Hz, Aβ: 36.7 ± 3.3 Hz, n = 7, p = 0.2891, Figure 5A) and charge transfer (control: 490.8 ± 50.8 pC, Aβ: 433.7 ± 82.6 pC, n = 7, p = 0.1875, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The Aβ effect on EPSC amplitude was prevented by the application of Cp since no remaining reduction in EPSC amplitude was found.
source: The Aβ effect on EPSC amplitude was prevented by the application of Cp since no remaining reduction in EPSC amplitude was found (control: 21.1 ± 3.1 pA, Aβ+Cp: 21.2 ± 4.8 pA, p = 0.3125, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: No changes were observed for EPSC frequency with application of Cp together with Aβ.
source: No changes were observed for EPSC frequency with application of Cp together with Aβ (control: 35.1 ± 7.4 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 34.1 ± 10.6 Hz, n = 5, p = 0.5, Figure 5B) as well as for charge transfer (control: 88.0 ± 18.4 pC, Aβ+Cp: 92.5 ± 34.6 pC, n = 5, p = 0.5, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: No changes were observed for EPSC charge transfer with application of Cp together with Aβ.
source: No changes were observed for EPSC frequency with application of Cp together with Aβ (control: 35.1 ± 7.4 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 34.1 ± 10.6 Hz, n = 5, p = 0.5, Figure 5B) as well as for charge transfer (control: 88.0 ± 18.4 pC, Aβ+Cp: 92.5 ± 34.6 pC, n = 5, p = 0.5, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The co-application of Aβ and Cp together with the TrpV1 receptor antagonist Cz (Aβ+Cp+Cz) blocked Cp's preventive effects since a 18.8 +/- 5.1% reduction in EPSC amplitude was observed.
source: As expected, the co-application of Aβ and Cp together with the TrpV1 receptor antagonist Cz (Aβ+Cp+Cz) blocked Cp's preventive effects since we observed a 18.8 +/- 5.1% reduction in EPSC amplitude (control: 19.8 ± 2.7 pA, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 15.9 ± 2.3 pA, n = 8, p = 0.0039, Figure 5C), indicating that TrpV1 receptor activation is mediating the preventive effect of Cp against the Aβ-induced effects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: TrpV1 receptor activation is mediating the preventive effect of Cp against the Aβ-induced effects on EPSC amplitude.
source: As expected, the co-application of Aβ and Cp together with the TrpV1 receptor antagonist Cz (Aβ+Cp+Cz) blocked Cp's preventive effects since we observed a 18.8 +/- 5.1% reduction in EPSC amplitude (control: 19.8 ± 2.7 pA, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 15.9 ± 2.3 pA, n = 8, p = 0.0039, Figure 5C), indicating that TrpV1 receptor activation is mediating the preventive effect of Cp against the Aβ-induced effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the TrpV1 antagonist blocks Cp's protective effect.

claim: No changes effected by Aβ+Cp+Cz treatment were observed for EPSC frequency.
source: No changes effected by Aβ+Cp+Cz treatment were observe for EPSC frequency (control: 30.7 ± 1.8 Hz, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 30.0 ± 3.6 Hz, n = 8, p = 0.3203, Figure 5C) and charge transfer (control: 350.0 ± 58.3 pC, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 288.8 ± 56.5 pC, n = 8, p = 0.0977, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: No changes effected by Aβ+Cp+Cz treatment were observed for EPSC charge transfer.
source: No changes effected by Aβ+Cp+Cz treatment were observe for EPSC frequency (control: 30.7 ± 1.8 Hz, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 30.0 ± 3.6 Hz, n = 8, p = 0.3203, Figure 5C) and charge transfer (control: 350.0 ± 58.3 pC, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 288.8 ± 56.5 pC, n = 8, p = 0.0977, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: 1 µM Aβ induced a 34.4 ± 5.4% reduction of IPSC amplitude.
source: Similarly to EPSCs, 1 µM Aβ induced a 34.4 ± 5.4% reduction of IPSC amplitude (control: 88.2 ± 15.8 pA, Aβ: 57.7 ± 10.3 pA, n = 9, p = 0.002, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aβ also induced a 32.5 ± 6.5% reduction of IPSC charge transfer.
source: Moreover, Aβ also induced a 32.5 ± 6.5% reduction of IPSC charge transfer (control: 1073.0 ± 183.8 pC, Aβ: 691.7 ± 101.1 pC, n = 9, p = 0.002, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No alterations following Aβ application was found on IPSC frequency.
source: No alterations following Aβ application was found on IPSC frequency (control: 23.9 ± 0.7 Hz, Aβ: 24.1 ± 1.0 Hz, n = 9, p = 0.2480, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cp did not prevent Aβ-induced alterations of IPSC parameters when recorded at Vh = 0 mV.
source: In contrast to EPSCs, Cp did not prevent Aβ-induced alterations of IPSC parameters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing persistent reductions in IPSC amplitude and charge transfer.

claim: A persistent 23.9 ± 9.4% reduction in IPSC amplitude was observed after Aβ+Cp treatment at Vh = 0 mV.
source: Our experiments evidenced a persistent 23.9 ± 9.4% reduction in IPSC amplitude (control: 71.37 ± 13.5 pA, Aβ+Cp: 55.4 ± 14.3 pA, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and a 30.3 ± 10.3% reduction in charge transfer (control: 1214 ± 238.8 pC, Aβ+Cp: 858.9 ± 205.1 pC, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A 30.3 ± 10.3% reduction in IPSC charge transfer was observed after Aβ+Cp treatment at Vh = 0 mV.
source: Our experiments evidenced a persistent 23.9 ± 9.4% reduction in IPSC amplitude (control: 71.37 ± 13.5 pA, Aβ+Cp: 55.4 ± 14.3 pA, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and a 30.3 ± 10.3% reduction in charge transfer (control: 1214 ± 238.8 pC, Aβ+Cp: 858.9 ± 205.1 pC, n = 6, p = 0.0156, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No changes in IPSC frequency were observed after Aβ+Cp treatment at Vh = 0 mV.
source: No changes in IPSC frequency were observed (control: 31.5 ± 2.4 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 29.5 ± 3.0 Hz, n = 6, p = 0.1094, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The TrpV1 receptor is a non-selective ion channel with high permeability to Ca2+.
source: The TrpV1 receptor is a non-selective ion channel with high permeability to Ca2+(Caterina et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TrpV1 supported by a citation.

claim: When recording IPSCs with a high-chloride intracellular solution at Vh = -70 mV, Aβ induced a 26.8 ± 10.4% reduction in IPSC amplitude.
source: The results showed no differences in the Aβ-effect on IPSCs since a 26.8 ± 10.4% reduction was found in amplitude (control: 62.9 ± 8.0 pA, Aβ: 44.4 ± 7.2 pA, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5D) and a 29.7 ± 7.7% reduction in charge transfer (control: 713.0 ± 115.8 pC, Aβ: 507.8 ± 122.7 pC, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: When recording IPSCs with a high-chloride intracellular solution at Vh = -70 mV, Aβ induced a 29.7 ± 7.7% reduction in IPSC charge transfer.
source: The results showed no differences in the Aβ-effect on IPSCs since a 26.8 ± 10.4% reduction was found in amplitude (control: 62.9 ± 8.0 pA, Aβ: 44.4 ± 7.2 pA, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5D) and a 29.7 ± 7.7% reduction in charge transfer (control: 713.0 ± 115.8 pC, Aβ: 507.8 ± 122.7 pC, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: No changes were observed in IPSC frequency when recording with high-chloride solution after Aβ application.
source: Similarly to prior experiments, no changes were observed in IPSC frequency (control: 21.8 ± 2.0 Hz, Aβ: 22.0 ± 2.6 Hz, n = 5, p = 0.5, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: 5 µM Cp completely prevented the Aβ-induced reduction in IPSC charge transfer when recording with high-chloride solution at Vh = -70 mV.
source: Nonetheless, under these conditions, we found that 5 µM Cp completely prevented the Aβ-induced reduction in IPSC charge transfer (control: 333.0 ± 112.0 pC, Aβ+Cp: 268.1 ± 103.3 pC, n = 6, p = 0.1563, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Cp partially prevented the Aβ-effect on IPSC amplitude since only a 12.7 ± 7.5% reduction was observed when recording with high-chloride solution at Vh = -70 mV.
source: In addition, Cp partially prevented the Aβ-effect on amplitude since only a 12.7 ± 7.5% reduction was observed (control: 130.3 ± 26.1 pA, Aβ+Cp: 107.7 ± 20.4 pA, n = 6, p = 0.0313, Figure 5E), in contrast to the 26.8 ± 10.4% reduction found with Aβ application alone (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: IPSC frequency remained unaltered after Aβ+Cp treatment when recording with high-chloride solution at Vh = -70 mV.
source: IPSC frequency remained unaltered (control: 17.4 ± 3.6 Hz, Aβ+Cp: 17.4 ± 3.5 Hz, n = 6, p = 0.2813, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Cp's preventive effect on IPSC parameters was mediated by TrpV1 receptor activation since a 34.3 ± 10.6% reduction in IPSC amplitude was observed with Aβ+Cp+Cz.
source: Finally, we performed experiments using the TrpV1 receptor antagonist Cz together with Aβ and Cp (Aβ+Cp+Cz). Our results demonstrate that Cp's preventive effect on IPSC parameters was mediated by TrpV1 receptor activation since we observed a 34.3 ± 10.6% reduction in IPSC amplitude (control: 75.4 ± 22.2 pA, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 41.8 ± 6.8 pA, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5F) and a 44.1 ± 7.5% reduction in charge transfer (control: 992.1 ± 457.3 pC, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 430.0 ± 126.8 pC, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: A 44.1 ± 7.5% reduction in IPSC charge transfer was observed with Aβ+Cp+Cz.
source: Finally, we performed experiments using the TrpV1 receptor antagonist Cz together with Aβ and Cp (Aβ+Cp+Cz). Our results demonstrate that Cp's preventive effect on IPSC parameters was mediated by TrpV1 receptor activation since we observed a 34.3 ± 10.6% reduction in IPSC amplitude (control: 75.4 ± 22.2 pA, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 41.8 ± 6.8 pA, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5F) and a 44.1 ± 7.5% reduction in charge transfer (control: 992.1 ± 457.3 pC, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 430.0 ± 126.8 pC, n = 5, p = 0.0313, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: No changes in IPSC frequency were observed with Aβ+Cp+Cz.
source: As expected, no changes in IPSC frequency were observed (control: 23.0 ± 5.9 Hz, Aβ+Cp+Cz: 19.7 ± 4.7 Hz, n = 5, p = 0.2188, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Cp treatment recovers the inhibitory input to CA3 PC via a postsynaptic mechanism involving Ca2+ influx through TrpV1 receptor activation.
source: This suggests that Cp treatment recovers the inhibitory input to CA3 PC via a postsynaptic mechanism involving Ca2+ influx through TrpV1 receptor activation since the Cp protective effect was absent when experiments were performed at Vh = 0 mV.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the protective effect depends on the holding potential.

claim: Cp prevents the Aβ-induced shift in excitatory/inhibitory current balance in hippocampal gamma oscillations induced with KA.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that Cp prevents the Aβ-induced shift in excitatory/inhibitory current balance in hippocampal gamma oscillations induced with KA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on EPSCs and IPSCs.

claim: Cp rescued impaired gamma power to levels similar to those recorded in control slices after 30 min treatment.
source: Gamma oscillation power measurements after Cp treatment application (30 min) showed that Cp rescued impaired gamma power to levels similar to those recorded in control slices at the same time point (control 30 min: 22.1 ± 3.7×10−9 V2, Aβ+Cp 30 min: 18.7 ± 3.9×10−9 V2, p = 0.2323, Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Slices incubated just with Aβ (with no Cp application), showed a persistently impaired gamma oscillation power.
source: In contrast, slices incubated just with Aβ (with no Cp application), showed a persistently impaired gamma oscillation power (Aβ 30 min: 9.9 ± 2.1×10−9 V2, p = 0.0018 vs control, Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A-D.

claim: The Cp rescue effect was TrpV1-dependent since the application of Cz together with Cp prevented the rescue of impaired gamma oscillation power.
source: Finally, we showed that the Cp rescue effect was TrpV1-dependent since the application of Cz together with Cp prevented the rescue of impaired gamma oscillation power (Aβ+Cp+ Cz 30 min: 11.1 ± 1.7×10−9 V2, p = 0.0074 vs control, Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A-D.

claim: TrpV1 activation is a promising therapeutic target for attempts to restore Aβ-impaired functional network dynamics and cellular mechanisms back to physiological levels.
source: Overall, our results suggest that TrpV1 activation is a promising therapeutic target for attempts to restore Aβ-impaired functional network dynamics and cellular mechanisms back to physiological levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing rescue effects.

claim: Whether this restoration of cognition-relevant network function translates to demonstrable cognitive benefit in vivo is the focus of ongoing studies.
source: Whether this restoration of cognition-relevant network function translates to demonstrable cognitive benefit in vivo is the focus of ongoing studies.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The function of TrpV1 in nociception and sensory transmission is well documented.
source: While the function of TrpV1 in nociception and sensory transmission is well documented, its role in CNS is less well understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TrpV1 function.

claim: The role of TrpV1 in CNS is less well understood.
source: While the function of TrpV1 in nociception and sensory transmission is well documented, its role in CNS is less well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Growing evidence suggests that TrpV1 is involved in several brain functions by modulating glial and neuronal activity in normal and pathological conditions.
source: Growing evidence suggests that TrpV1 is involved in several brain functions by modulating glial and neuronal activity in normal and pathological conditions (Edwards, 2014; Ho et al., 2012; Martins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cannabinoid receptor activation is unable to protect cognition-relevant functional network dynamics against Aβ-induced impairment.
source: In this study, we found that cannabinoid receptor activation is unable to protect cognition-relevant functional network dynamics against Aβ-induced impairment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: TrpV1 activation by Cp displayed strong protective and restorative properties, preventing and rescuing the Aβ-induced degradation of hippocampal gamma oscillations and relevant cellular mechanisms.
source: Conversely, TrpV1 activation by Cp displayed strong protective and restorative properties, preventing and rescuing the Aβ-induced degradation of hippocampal gamma oscillations and relevant cellular mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Benito et al. (2012) have reported that Aβ can induce a pathological inflammatory response in primary astrocyte cultures in which several membrane receptors, including TrpV1, are involved.
source: In contrast to the preventive role of TrpV1 activation found here, Benito et al. (2012) have reported that Aβ can induce a pathological inflammatory response in primary astrocyte cultures in which several membrane receptors, including TrpV1, are involved.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The differing consequences of TrpV1 activation could be explained by the different Aβ preparations and concentrations used in different studies.
source: These differing consequences of TrpV1 activation could be explained by the different Aβ preparations and concentrations used in both studies: our Aβ preparation contains a mix of different aggregation states (monomers, oligomers, fibrils; Kurudenkandy et al., 2014) while Benito and coworkers used a purely fibrillar Aβ preparation (Benito et al., 2012), which is more toxic in our experimental model (Kurudenkandy et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing different experimental conditions and prior research.

claim: TrpV1 is known to play an important role in anti-inflammatory processes.
source: Since TrpV1 is known to play an important role in anti-inflammatory processes (Devesa et al., 2011; Tsuji and Aono, 2012) it is possible that the effect of 5 µM fibrillar Aβ induces a pathological activation of inflammatory mechanisms in the primary astrocytes culture.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that the effect of 5 µM fibrillar Aβ induces a pathological activation of inflammatory mechanisms in the primary astrocytes culture.
source: Since TrpV1 is known to play an important role in anti-inflammatory processes (Devesa et al., 2011; Tsuji and Aono, 2012) it is possible that the effect of 5 µM fibrillar Aβ induces a pathological activation of inflammatory mechanisms in the primary astrocytes culture.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism underlying different experimental results.

claim: Hyperactivation of immune responses (neuroinflammation) induced by Aβ has been shown in other studies.
source: Hyperactivation of immune responses (neuroinflammation) induced by Aβ has also been shown in other studies (Blasko et al., 2004; Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TrpV1 activation as a therapeutic target has been tested in a mouse model of ischemia.
source: On the other hand, similar to our study, TrpV1 activation as a therapeutic target has been tested in a mouse model of ischemia (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cao and coworkers found that TrpV1 activation leads to a decrease in the volume of affected brain tissue after the induction of cerebral ischemia.
source: Cao and coworkers found that TrpV1 activation leads to a decrease in the volume of affected brain tissue after the induction of cerebral ischemia.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: An improvement in a behavioral-neurofunction-test score was found in animals treated with Cp after brain ischemia.
source: Furthermore, an improvement in a behavioral-neurofunction-test score was found in animals treated with Cp after brain ischemia.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TrpV1 activation in astrocytes in a rat model of Parkinson's disease is involved in the prevention of dopamine neuron degeneration in substantia nigra.
source: Another recent study has also reported that TrpV1 activation in astrocytes in a rat model of Parkinson's disease is involved in the prevention of dopamine neuron degeneration in substantia nigra (Nam et al., 2015).
